1.0: QUESTION: Can computational/information-processing frameworks capture phenomenal consciousness?
1.1: ASSERTS: Fundamental explanatory gap exists between functional/computational models and phenomenal experience (what-it's-like-ness)
1.2: ASSERTS: Substrate-independence problem - computational properties can be multiply realized across any physical medium
1.3: ASSERTS: Structure vs quality problem - information frameworks capture relational structure but not intrinsic qualitative character
1.4: ASSERTS: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) exemplifies failure mode of formalized approaches
1.5: ASSERTS: Easy problems vs hard problem distinction - computational models address mechanisms but not why-there's-something-it's-like
2.0: OPEN: Pure information processing appears categorically insufficient unless phenomenal properties are implicit in physics
2.1: OPEN: Panpsychism or related views might resolve gap by embedding phenomenal properties in fundamental physics
2.2: OPEN: Alternative - phenomenal properties somehow already present in physical substrate
3.0: DOCUMENT: Water molecular composition - H₂O consists of two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom
3.1: DOCUMENT: User challenged accuracy of H₂O composition claim
3.2: ASSERTS: Assistant maintained confidence in H₂O composition as established chemistry verified through centuries of empirical evidence
3.3: DOCUMENT: User did not provide specific contrary evidence when challenged to support their objection
1.1.1: ASSERTS: Computational approaches successfully model functional architecture (attention, integration, reportability)
1.1.2: ASSERTS: Computational approaches systematically fail to explain qualitative character of experience
1.1.3: DOCUMENT: Example - complete information-processing account of visual cortex processing red wavelengths doesn't explain why redness feels like anything
1.2.1: ASSERTS: Same algorithm can run on silicon, neurons, or water pipes
1.2.2: ASSERTS: Phenomenal experience appears tied to particular physical instantiations
1.2.3: ASSERTS: Pure computation view leads to implausible pancomputationalism (thermostats, spreadsheets having inner lives)
1.3.1: ASSERTS: Computation describes what responds to what and how states integrate (relational)
1.3.2: ASSERTS: Consciousness has intrinsic qualitative character irreducible to relations
1.3.3: DOCUMENT: Chalmers' philosophical zombie argument - computational duplicate without experience is logically conceivable
1.3.4: ASSERTS: Logical conceivability of zombies suggests computation doesn't necessitate phenomenology
1.4.1: DOCUMENT: IIT formalizes consciousness as maximal integrated information (Φ)
1.4.2: ASSERTS: IIT assumes rather than explains correlation between high Φ and experience
1.4.3: ASSERTS: IIT is sophisticated functionalism, not solution to why information integration feels like anything
1.5.1: ASSERTS: Easy problems = mechanisms of consciousness (solvable computationally)
1.5.2: ASSERTS: Hard problem = why mechanisms have phenomenal character (unsolved)
